 UPSC Chairman Ajay Kumar on AI in education, India's talent ambitions and the future of jobs 
 UPSC Chairman Dr Ajay Kumar discusses how India can strengthen its position in the global AI landscape through regional language models, robust data infrastructure and advanced AI skills. In an exclusive interaction with ETEducation, he also shares insights on AI adoption in education, changing employment trends and the importance of nurturing creativity and critical thinking.  UPSC Chairman Dr Ajay Kumar Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing the skills required in the workplace, the way students learn and how institutions prepare the next generation of professionals. For India, the challenge extends beyond adopting AI tools to building the talent, research capabilities and technological infrastructure needed to emerge as a global AI leader. In an exclusive interaction with ETEducation, Dr Ajay Kumar , Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and author of AI Nation: Bharat's Path to AI Power, discusses India's opportunities in the evolving AI landscape, the role of regional languages and small language models, and the need to strengthen the country's data infrastructure. He also shares his perspective on AI adoption in higher education, developing advanced AI skills at scale, the future of employment and how educational institutions must nurture creativity, originality and the ability to ask the right questions. Q. In your book, AI Nation: Bharat’s Path to AI Power , you argue that AI is making the world increasingly unequal. How can India avoid becoming merely a consumer of AI technology and emerge as a global leader? Dr Ajay Kumar: India should avoid trying to compete with the US and China on the sheer scale of AI capabilities, as these countries are far ahead of the rest of the world. Instead, we should focus on areas where we have natural strengths. One such area is language. The capabilities of large language models in several Indian regional languages remain limited outside India. We have the linguistic diversity and knowledge base to develop these capabilities, and companies such as Sarvam and initiatives such as Bhasini are already working in this direction. Another priority could be developing AI solutions for unique problems and challenges of India and the wider developing world. This could include healthcare challenges such as tuberculosis, or agricultural problems faced by developing economies. We could also focus on small language models (SLMs) that can operate on edge devices, enabling decentralised applications. SLM market is still evolving, and India has an opportunity to take a leadership role. With our chip-design capabilities, nearly a billion smartphones and a growing consumer electronics market, India has an opportunity to develop solutions that can power smart devices of the future. India should also take a leadership role in shaping global AI standards. The AI Summit in India has created an opportunity for us to contribute to global AI standards from the perspective of the developing world. We should ensure that AI governance standards reflect the concerns and priorities of the Global South. Network-based technologies naturally lead to a concentration of power and wealth. While this tendency cannot be wished away, focusing on these areas can help India create its own space and leadership in technological capability. Q. Your book places considerable emphasis on data as a source of national power. How can we use this data as a source of strength and gain an advantage in the AI ecosystem? Dr Ajay Kumar: A large proportion of the data generated in India is not stored within the country. We generate an estimated 20% of the world's data, but our data storage capacity accounts for only around 1–2% of global capacity. As a result, a substantial share of our data goes outside India. The financial sector is an exception, where payment-related data has to be stored in India. Therefore, one of the first requirements is to build greater data centre capacity. India had around 900 MW of data centre capacity, but there is now a conscious effort to attract investment and expand this infrastructure. We are looking at a significant increase, with the capacity potentially doubling over the next three to four years. However, storing data in India is only one part of the solution. We also need mechanisms through which data can be used to create value for the people who own it. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act provides the legal framework, while the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) offers a consent-based framework for sharing data. The next step is to ensure that DEPA is actively implemented across sectors, including agriculture, education and healthcare. So far, its use has been more visible in the financial sector through account aggregators. We need a mission-mode approach to expand the use of this framework, much like the efforts made for digital payments. Data, when used meaningfully, can create huge value. We have the legal framework and the foundational architecture; the challenge now is to scale their adoption and overcome the initial hesitation around data sharing. Q. Your book makes a strong case for building India's AI capabilities through infrastructure, innovation and skilled human capital. Is India's education ecosystem prepared to produce the talent required for AI research and innovation? Dr Ajay Kumar: I would look at this from the experience of introducing computers in schools. When I was serving as IT Secretary in Kerala, we introduced computers in schools through the IT@School project in 2008–09 and made computer education mandatory. At that time, there were concerns about whether a diverse country like India, with villages, small towns, government schools and private institutions, would be able to provide computer education to all children. However, the adoption of technology gradually expanded across the country, including in states that were not as advanced technologically. Our education systems have generally been quick to adopt technology. Today, learning is no longer limited to classrooms. Students in the best schools as well as children in villages are accessing online learning platforms. This is creating a certain degree of a level playing field in access to educational resources. AI is an even more disruptive technology, and I have little doubt that schools and educational institutions will adopt and adapt to it. There is no real choice in the matter. Q. UPSC is India's largest recruitment body. With the increasing influence of AI, could the Commission use AI to assess candidates differently? Dr Ajay Kumar: UPSC is already using AI in several parts of its administrative and recruitment processes. For instance, we use it to identify duplicate candidature applications, which would be extremely difficult to do manually given the large number of applications we receive. AI also helps us scrutinise lakhs of documents submitted by candidates. We use face authentication at examination centres to prevent impersonation. Another application is in knowledge management, where technology helps us analyse similar disciplinary cases and maintain consistency in the penalties recommended. Such comparisons across several years of cases would be difficult to carry out manually. However, we have not used AI for the evaluation of candidates, and we do not believe that the solutions available today can match the robustness of our existing human evaluation systems. The skills, knowledge and competencies expected from candidates evolve with time, and AI is now an important domain; AI-related questions find a place during recruitment examinations. But the evaluation itself continues to be manual and will continue to be manual. As of now, UPSC has no plans to introduce AI for candidate evaluation. Q. Several state governments are announcing AI policies and initiatives to promote AI literacy in schools . Is this a welcome step, and what more needs to be done? Dr Ajay Kumar: AI literacy is essential. If we look at the pace of technological adoption, the internet spread across the world faster than earlier technologies such as electricity and the steam engine. Mobile phones expanded even faster, followed by social media platforms. AI has moved at an even greater speed. Technologies that were largely confined to research communities until recently are now being used by ordinary people through widely accessible platforms. Governments and educational institutions will have to respond to this change. At the school level, I have little doubt that AI literacy will become part of education. The bigger challenge, however, is developing advanced AI skills at scale. India should aim to become a supplier of AI talent for the world, while also meeting its own requirements. We need to look beyond training a few hundred or a few thousand people. The scale should be millions. The growth of India's IT outsourcing industry was supported by coding training reaching smaller cities and communities across the country. We need a similar broad-based effort for AI, covering the different kinds of advanced skills that the technology will require. If we can build this talent pool, India can create opportunities for its own economy and supply skilled professionals to the world. Q. There are concerns that AI could take away jobs, particularly entry-level roles. Is this a genuine concern, and how should India's youth prepare for an AI-driven future? Dr Ajay Kumar: The answer is both yes and no. Some jobs will certainly be lost, but many new jobs will also be created. There will also be roles in which people will need to retrain and learn to perform their work differently. At UPSC, for example, the introduction of face authentication and AI-based deduplication has enabled us to undertake tasks that were earlier difficult to perform. These systems create a need for people with technology-related skills, but also for non-technical professionals who can manage and operate the new systems. The larger opportunity lies in using AI to solve problems that were earlier considered impossible to address. AI can process data at a scale that was difficult to imagine earlier, opening up possibilities in areas such as healthcare, space, the oceans and the human body. For instance, the CEO of Anthropic recently made a statement suggesting that cancer could become history in a decade. Whether or not that prediction comes true, it illustrates the scale of possibilities that AI could open up. The opportunity, therefore, is not limited to creating employment through new technologies; it is also about creating value by solving problems that have affected humanity for generations. If we can solve such challenges, the impact on millions of lives could be far greater than the number of jobs directly created in the process. Q. What is your message to education leaders and policymakers working to create an AI-ready ecosystem for students? Dr Ajay Kumar: We have to recognise that AI is here and will disrupt traditional ways of doing things. The most important thing is to ensure that AI serves human goals and objectives. From the perspective of education, one of the most important responsibilities is to teach students how to ask the right questions. The ability to ask the right questions is what future education should be all about. Information will be widely available, and AI will make processing that information easier. While teaching the basics will remain important, access to information and the ability to process it will no longer be the biggest challenges. What education must nurture is creativity and originality — the ability to think differently and ask questions that others may not think of. That is where the responsibility of educational institutions and policymakers lies. Comments
